title: Palantir Seen Beating Revenue Estimates, Raising Guidance, Oppenheimer Says
detail:

Palantir Seen Beating Revenue Estimates, Raising Guidance, Oppenheimer Says
MT Newswires
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 12:48 PM EDT 1 min read
PLTR
OPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) is poised for another revenue beat and annual guidance raise in its upcoming Q3 report, with continued commercial and government strength driving a solid quarter, Oppenheimer said in a Thursday note.

The company is scheduled to report its Q3 results Monday.

Oppenheimer expects US commercial revenue growth of more than 140% and total government growth of more than 65%, supported by new-customer adoption, broader deployments of its AI Platform, and sustained demand for defense and mission-critical applications, according to the note.

The firm said it remains constructive on both commercial expansion and government demand, with governance, reliability, and sensitive data handling reinforcing the company's competitive positioning.

Palantir's differentiation comes from connecting fragmented enterprise systems into an operational framework, rather than providing another model or analytics tool, according to the note.

Replicating such an architecture would require multiple products and substantial rebuilding, supporting the view that switching costs deepen as customers integrate additional operational workflows, Oppenheimer said.

Oppenheimer maintained its outperform rating and raised its price target to $235 from $200.

Shares of Palantir were down more than 1% in Thursday afternoon trading.

title: What a $1,000 Investment in Palantir Could Be Worth by the End of 2027 (The Answer May Surprise You)

What a $1,000 Investment in Palantir Could Be Worth by the End of 2027 (The Answer May Surprise You)

Trading disclosure

Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been among the top artificial intelligence stocks to invest in for a while. It has delivered strong returns year after year, although 2026 has been an exception. It has risen only about 10% this year, which is disappointing compared to prior years. However, those who are bullish on Palantir may interpret this as a period of consolidation for the stock, one that's positioning it for an incredible 2027.

But is this true, or is there something else going on with Palantir? I think there's more to this story, and I'd suggest that investing in the stock right now might not be the best idea.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir is growing at a strong pace

Palantir develops AI-powered data analytics software that helps its users deliver actionable insights from live data streams. This software was originally marketed to the U.S. government and was eventually sold to other allied nations. Palantir established a major foothold as a service provider to the government sector, and eventually expanded its reach to the commercial market. Its products have been hugely successful there, and its latest success has been driven by its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which allows users to deploy AI agents.

Palantir's software integrates smoothly with the most widely used business systems, and in an environment where many companies are looking for ways to adopt and implement AI, its top line has been growing rapidly.

PLTR Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts.

Despite forecasts that its revenue growth would slow, Palantir continues to outperform expectations quarter after quarter. We'll see what its third-quarter results look like in a few weeks, but as of Q2, Palantir's growth rate was still accelerating.

Another bonus for Palantir shareholders is that it isn't a growth-at-all-costs company. During Q2, its profit margin was an incredible 55%. There were no weird accounting tricks being used, either -- that was actual profit that Palantir was generating. For investors who only want to invest in companies with positive cash flows, that impressive result will look attractive.

Between the high-growth investors and the positive-cash-flow investors, there's an army of investors who would find these shares potentially appealing, which is probably why Palantir's stock has held up as well as it has this year. However, there's one glaring red flag, and it could lead to a disappointing performance going forward.

title: What Did Snowflake Stock Investors Miss Before The Run?

What Did Snowflake Stock Investors Miss Before The Run?

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Snowflake (SNOW) stock returned 140.7% from April 29 to October 28, 2026, more than doubling a holder's money in six months. On its September 2 call, management said sales growth had sped up for a third straight quarter, with new AI products supplying about half of the speed-up. Over the six months before April 29, however, the shares had lost 47.6%. What had management been saying before then?

Snowflake Twice Told Investors Business Was Strong

Management held both calls before that decline began. The upbeat remarks came first, and the drop followed. On the November 20, 2024 call, management said growth in the core business had "outperformed." The company also said the backlog of signed contracts not yet booked as sales had grown 55% from a year earlier, and that this growth was accelerating. Because this backlog turns into sales later, a reader could have taken the metric as demand running ahead of the reported figures.

On the August 27, 2025 call, management said the core business remained very strong. Net revenue retention, which tracks what existing customers spend compared with a year earlier, was 125%, against 127% on the 2024 call. The commentary was upbeat, but retention had slipped slightly between the two calls.

Snowflake's Growth Picked Up Again Before April

Snowflake's AI work showed up next, though only in product launches. On December 18, 2025, Equilar's ExecAtlas was named a launch partner for Snowflake Intelligence, the company's enterprise intelligence agent. That announcement showed what Snowflake was building, not what it was selling.

The first sign in the figures followed. In the quarter ended January 31, 2026, filed on March 20, revenue grew 30.1% from a year earlier. This compared with 28.7% in the quarter ended October 2025. A single quarter was hard to read as a turn, because growth had been 31.8% in the quarter ended July 2025. Management had already reported that quarter on its February 25 call, nearly a month before the filing, so the sign was there to catch then, though it was not yet a pattern.

The six months that followed established that pattern. The S&P 500 gained 9.1% over the run from April 29. Among three large peers, Microsoft performed best with 25.6%, while Amazon lost 3.2% and Alphabet lost 7.0%, so the run belonged to Snowflake rather than to its group. Snowflake's revenue growth revenue growth rose again in each of the next two quarters, reaching 35.1% in the quarter ended July 31, 2026. That is a figure for the whole company, not a single product line. The run's two biggest one-day gains, 36.5% on May 28 and 16.6% on September 3, each came the day after a quarterly report.

title: Why Is Everybody Paying A Premium For Palantir Stock?
detail:
Why Is Everybody Paying A Premium For Palantir Stock?
Trefis Team

PLTR
^GSPC
MSFT
AMZN
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Shares of Palantir Technologies (PLTR) trade at 156.6 times its earnings over the last twelve months, compared with 22.6 times for the S&P 500. Because Palantir already makes a large profit on its sales, that valuation looks like a bet on how far those sales can still grow. So which part of Palantir's business are buyers paying up for?

Palantir Is Growing Fastest With Domestic Commercial Customers

On the August 3, 2026 call, management said revenue from U.S. commercial customers grew 149% from a year earlier in the second quarter of 2026, reaching $764 million. In the same quarter, Palantir's government business as a whole grew 79%, and total revenue grew 92.8%.

Management says the demand comes from companies seeking sovereign AI. These customers want full control of the data, logic and security behind the AI they build on Palantir's AIP platform. Palantir finished the quarter with 653 U.S. commercial customers, 35% more than a year earlier.

How Fast Would Palantir Have To Grow?

At this price, just to maintain its $472 billion market value with no return on top, Palantir would have to grow its revenue 33.6% a year for seven years. At a mature P/E of 28.8, supporting that value would require $16.4 billion of yearly profit. Assuming a net margin of 35%, Palantir would need $46.9 billion of revenue to earn it. That revenue requirement is 7.61 times the $6.16 billion Palantir took in over the twelve months to June 2026. We place that margin just under halfway between the company's average of 23.1% and its peak of 49.0% over the last twelve quarter ends. We use a timeline of seven years, our longest horizon, because Palantir's P/E today is 5.44 times the mature one.

Like the margin and the horizon, the mature P/E is a Trefis assumption. We assign 60% of its weight to 28.0, our level for software companies. The other 40% would go to Palantir's own average P/E of 246.0 over the last twelve quarter ends. Because that historical average is so high, we use 30 in its place.

Can Palantir Keep Growing That Fast?

Management expects so for 2026. On the August 3 call, management raised its revenue guide to between $8.15 billion and $8.16 billion, an amount 82.2% more than in 2025. It also expects U.S. commercial revenue to grow at least 134% in 2026, faster than the company as a whole. After 2026, Palantir would still have to grow 30.9% a year for six and a half more years. That is slower than the guide, but the company must sustain it for far longer.

Palantir has not always grown that fast. In the twelve months to June 2023 it grew 17.2%, against 78.9% in the twelve months to June 2026.

The required growth is most sensitive to how many years Palantir has. Evaluated over five years instead of seven, Palantir would have to grow 50.1% a year. If the company kept the 49.0% net margin of its latest twelve months, it would need 27.4% a year, but that margin is its highest at any quarter end since mid-2020.

For today's price to hold, Palantir would have to keep its U.S. commercial business growing for years after 2026 while maintaining most of today's margin. If growth slips back toward its pace of a few years ago, Palantir would need more years, and the stock becomes a riskier bet. Revenue growth from U.S. commercial customers is the measure to watch when Palantir reports in November 2026.

How Much Palantir Technologies Do You Already Own?

If you own an S&P 500 or Nasdaq fund, you already own Palantir Technologies, alongside the same few giants that lead those funds. Since its inception in September 2020 it has returned 105%, ahead of a benchmark that combines the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap and Russell 2000.

Nebius Is Up 103% in 2026 Despite Musk's "Guppy-Level Death" Warning: Take Profits, or Buy More? ©@putilich from Getty Images via Canva, @Cnv Studio from CnvStudio's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Nebius stock is up 103% in 2026, helped by an August report in which second-quarter revenue rose 454% to $582.3 million.

Its October slide came from debt fears that started at CoreWeave and spread to every AI cloud, capped by Elon Musk's warning, more than from bad news at Nebius.

Contracts with Microsoft and Meta back Nebius's borrowing and Palantir added a new sales channel, but analysts expect its capex to reach $29.1 billion in 2027.

At about 6.5x forward sales, with estimates holding, the stock is worth buying for investors who can sit through big swings, as long as November's report shows customers still paying up front.

Nebius Group (NBIS:NASDAQ) is up 103% in 2026 through Wednesday's close, even after falling about 23% since Sept. 30 as investors soured on AI cloud companies that run on borrowed money.

NBIS Stock Price: Year-to-Date 2026 (TIKR)

The scare started at CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ), and on Oct. 25 SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk posted on X that more than 200 neoclouds are "going to see guppy-level death and consolidation." Musk isn't neutral: SpaceX runs its own data centers and sells computing capacity. Nebius says it has "investment-grade customer commitments of more than $40 billion of long-term contracts," including Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ). In September, Palantir (PLTR:NASDAQ) named it its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner.

The August Report Kept the Rally Going

Before the open on Aug. 12, Nebius reported its second quarter:

Revenue up 454% to $582.3 million

Adjusted EBITDA of $236.2 million, a 41% margin, against a $21.0 million loss a year earlier

Four new AI cloud deals averaging more than $1 billion each

The stock jumped 34% that day.

A month later, Palantir added a channel: it will offer Nebius's compute to commercial customers running their own models.

October's Selloff Started at CoreWeave

Worries about CoreWeave's debt hit Nebius hard on Oct. 16, though the two balance sheets looked nothing alike. At June 30, Nebius's borrowings net of cash came to about $0.5 billion, excluding leases, against about $29.5 billion at CoreWeave on the same basis.

On Oct. 22, Nebius announced a $3.5 billion, 364-day secured facility from Citi, priced at SOFR plus 2.75% and stepping up to as much as 3.5%.

Musk says that window is closing. Debt markets, he wrote, have "almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers."
